The problem is that they (gov't, comcast, et all) can monitor the origin IP to VPN and see that you are connected to the VPN. They can also monitor VPN to destination to see that someone connected to the VPN connected to the destination. However, without logs provided by the VPN provider (assuming they're serving multiple customers) there's no way to determine that the origin IP and the destination IP were the two in communication with each other via the VPN. Even if they can link the CTO to the origin and destination IPs, it's still circumstantial unless they can determine that the CTO was the one actually making those requests through the VPN. For that, they'd have to get the data from the VPN provider. While I doubt that most VPN services are setup with a sophisticate certificate authority and strict verification of the certifications at connect time, the amount of work to constantly monitor and intercept that traffic would be burdensome to the extreme and if it was exposed (which would be fairly trivial to determine) would also lead to further erosion of world sentiment toward US surveillance activity.

Government surveilled or otherwise, use a provider that supports OpenVPN with certificates, make sure they are their own certificate authority, make sure they keep their keys secure, verify the certificate against the CA, and make sure your provider has enough customers to provide plausible deniability.
